archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A quarterback whose value this year comes less from the pocket than from turning broken dropbacks into scramble first downs, paired with a passing game that works between the hashes at intermediate depth and little else.

report.headline: Legs are carrying a passing game that hasn't recovered its 2024 form
report.take:
Daniels arrived as one of the league's most efficient young quarterbacks. His 2024 line ranked 11th in EPA per play at 0.204, with a 69% completion rate, and he ran for 891 yards. The two seasons since have told a different story. In 2025 he went 2-5 in seven games with a -2.7 CPOE, ranking 45th of 65 in that stat. In 2026's two logged games the passing has been worse by the box score: 5.1 yards per attempt ranks 40th of 42, and he is completing 56.9%. His 0.079 EPA per dropback still sits a respectable 22nd, and the gap between those two pictures is the whole story of his season.

The gap is his legs. He has scrambled on 14.5% of dropbacks: nine scrambles for 98 yards, 0.785 EPA each and six first downs. That is where the value is coming from. The pocket profile has also changed shape. His time to throw jumped to 3.25 seconds from 2.68 and 2.79 the last two years, yet his pressure-to-sack rate fell to 9.1%, third-best, after two seasons in the bottom tier at roughly 41-44%. He is holding the ball longer and escaping instead of going down. On 62 dropbacks that is a hint rather than a new identity, but it is the right trade: the scrambles more than pay for the extra hang time.

The raw numbers hide a lopsided passing chart. His eight throws behind the line cost -0.865 EPA apiece, which is screens and swings dying on contact. His 12 intermediate throws produced 0.676 EPA with an 18-point CPOE. Deep shots have hit 2 of 9. The short game (22 attempts, -10.2 CPOE) is where the accuracy problem lives. His bad-throw rate of 15.7% ranks 28th of 32 and matches his 14% career norm, so the misses are not new. His only efficient targets have been Stefon Diggs and Terry McLaurin. Everyone else, including Rachaad White, Dyami Brown and John Bates, is underwater per target, and McLaurin is currently out with a hamstring.

The immediate question is health. He dislocated his left elbow, and his snap share dropped to 55% in Week 2. Washington is aiming for a full practice week and a start against the Giants. Marcus Mariota, who started Week 4, is doubtful with an MCL sprain, so the depth chart behind Daniels is thin. If he plays, the matchup suits what he does. If he is limited or rusty, there is no good fallback.

strengths.title: Scrambles turning broken plays positive
strengths.body: He is escaping on one of every seven dropbacks and moving the chains on two-thirds of those scrambles. His 891 rushing yards as a rookie show the running ability is real. The scramble EPA will cool off a sample of nine, but the scrambling should remain a core part of his value as long as the elbow doesn't make him play it safe.

strengths.title: Sacks avoided despite longer holds
strengths.body: Two years of bottom-tier pressure-to-sack rates have flipped to third-best, even as his time to throw rose by more than half a second. The cause looks like a deliberate choice to escape rather than absorb the sack, which is the right lesson. Expect the rate to drift up toward league norms, but probably not back to 41-44%.

strengths.title: Intermediate window is open
strengths.body: Between 10 and 19 air yards he has been accurate and productive, at 58% success and +18 CPOE. Those are mostly Diggs and McLaurin routes. It is a small sample of 12 throws, but it is the area of the field this offense should build around.

concerns.title: Accuracy hasn't come back since 2024
concerns.body: His tracking CPOE of -2.78 nearly matches his 2025 mark, so two straight seasons now look more like his level than his rookie year does. Short throws are the main leak, and the bad-throw rate sits in the bottom five of 32. This is the flaw that limits his ceiling, and it is not a small-sample blip.

concerns.title: Target tree thins without McLaurin
concerns.body: Only Diggs and McLaurin have produced positive EPA per target. McLaurin is out, Rachaad White is out but expected to practice, and the next options have been actively harmful. The supporting cast is a big reason the yards per attempt sit near the bottom of the league.

concerns.title: Elbow and dead-end designed runs
concerns.body: He is coming off a dislocated elbow, his last logged game ended at 55% of snaps, and his three designed runs were all failures. The scramble value is instinctive, but the called runs have not worked. A cautious staff may trim them further, which costs little except as a constraint on the defense.

trend.note: Week 1 at Philadelphia was the good version: 3.9 pass EPA and two touchdowns while covering as a 6-point underdog. Week 2 at Dallas was cut short at 55% of snaps, with the value coming almost entirely from 69 rushing yards. Then came the elbow, so there is no stable trend line yet.

nextGame.headline: Giants can't pressure him, but they won't let him go deep
nextGame.body:
New York's defense is middling overall, ranked 20th in EPA. The relevant details cut both ways. The Giants generate almost no pressure, ranking 31st in hit rate and dead last in sack rate. That means clean pockets for a quarterback who is holding the ball 3.25 seconds, though it also means fewer broken plays to scramble out of. They are excellent at preventing explosive passes: 5th in explosive pass rate and 3rd in deep EPA. That shuts down the deep game, where Daniels has completed 2 of 9 anyway. Their run defense leaks explosives, ranking 29th, which suits his scrambles. They also allow 2.25 touchdowns per game to quarterbacks, 26th in the league, even while holding them to 220.5 yards.

Availability drives everything here. Daniels himself is the first question, and with Mariota doubtful there is no proven backup if the elbow isn't right. McLaurin and guard Sam Cosmi, a 98%-snap starter, are both out. Cosmi's absence would hurt more against a better rush than this one. On the Giants' side, edge Chauncey Golston and safety Jason Pinnock are both questionable. Losing Golston would weaken an already toothless rush, and losing Pinnock would test a back end that has been the defense's strength.

keyMatchups.title: Clean pockets versus a dead rush
keyMatchups.body: The Giants rank last in sack rate and 31st in hit rate. That gives Daniels time to work the intermediate throws where he has been most effective. The cost is fewer pressured dropbacks for him to scramble out of.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots into a top-3 deep defense
keyMatchups.body: New York ranks 3rd in deep EPA allowed, and Daniels has completed only 22% of his throws of 20-plus yards. Expect a dink-and-scramble plan. That puts pressure on the short accuracy that has been his weak spot.

keyMatchups.title: Red-zone touchdowns available
keyMatchups.body: The Giants allow 2.25 passing touchdowns per game to quarterbacks. All three of Daniels' touchdown passes came on 14 red-zone throws. Touchdowns, rather than yards, are the realistic route to a big fantasy line.

nextGame.watch: Whether he scrambles freely or stays in the pocket. Hesitancy to run would be the clearest sign the elbow is limiting him.

restOfSeason.body:
Assuming he holds up physically, the 5.1 yards per attempt should rise. The behind-the-line throws won't stay at -0.865 EPA forever, McLaurin's return restores a second reliable target, and his 2025 floor was 6.71. Still, two years of negative CPOE argue against a return to 2024's 7.4. The realistic version is a mid-pack passer at roughly 6.3-6.8 yards per attempt, with his rushing pushing him into the top half for fantasy and overall EPA.

Some numbers will regress. The near-zero sack rate will creep up, and the scramble EPA will fall from 0.785 toward something good but ordinary. The zero interceptions are unlikely to hold for a player who threw nine as a rookie. The scramble rate itself looks sustainable, and that is the floor of his value.
swingFactors: Elbow health and willingness to scramble

bets.reason: The line assumes a healthy Daniels, but he is coming off a dislocated elbow with a doubtful backup behind him. McLaurin and Cosmi are out, and Washington is 0-2 in his logged starts with an offense 29th in success rate. Laying a field goal leaves no margin for any of that going wrong.

Both offenses rank in the bottom third for EPA: Washington 21st, New York 23rd. The Giants pass 10% less than expected, 30th in the league, which drains the clock. Their defense ranks 5th in explosive pass rate and 3rd in deep EPA, which removes Washington's quick-strike plays.

New York ranks 29th in explosive run rate allowed, and his scrambles have produced 0.785 EPA each. The risk is that a nonexistent Giants rush produces fewer broken plays and that the elbow makes him cautious. Treat it as a lean only if he practices fully.

The Giants allow 2.25 quarterback touchdowns per game, 26th in the league, while holding passers to 220.5 yards. Daniels has thrown all three of his touchdowns from the red zone. This matchup favors touchdowns more than yardage.

confidence.note: Only 62 dropbacks across two logged games, he is coming off an elbow dislocation, and his top receiver is out.
